# Artificial Intelligence (AI): a structured overview (with sourced pointers)

## Scope and limitations
This report is an evidence-backed overview built **only** from the sources that were successfully retrieved/extracted during research. Several important areas could not be fully sourced due to retrieval/extraction limits (notably: classic AI subfields beyond modern ML/LLMs; parts of AI history; the full text of the EU AI Act; and some UNESCO/EU/NIST PDFs). Those unresolved items are listed explicitly in **Unresolved / not fully sourced**.

## 1) What “AI” means (definitions)
### OECD (AI system definition)
OECD provides an updated AI-system definition and explains the update (including how it applies to generative AI systems such as large language models). OECD’s explainer page includes the definition text, describing an AI system as a *machine-based system* that, for human-defined objectives, *infers from inputs how to generate outputs* (including **predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions**) that can influence physical or virtual environments, with varying levels of autonomy/adaptiveness after deployment.

- Source: OECD, “AI system definition update” (definition text + rationale): <https://oecd.ai/en/wonk/ai-system-definition-update>

### NIST (AI definition)
NIST’s CSRC glossary defines **artificial intelligence** as a machine-based system that, for human-defined objectives, makes predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments.

- Source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “Artificial intelligence”: <https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/artificial_intelligence>

### NIST (where trustworthy-AI terminology is being developed)
NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework (AIRC) site also maintains a glossary hub and notes the release of a beta “Language of Trustworthy AI” glossary.

- Source: NIST AIRC Glossary hub: <https://airc.nist.gov/glossary/>

**Important missing piece:** this source set did **not** yield extractable, authoritative NIST (or equivalent) definitions for **machine learning** and **deep learning**, nor a single authoritative quote establishing the common hierarchy **AI ⊃ ML ⊃ DL**.

## 2) A minimal history (milestones that could be sourced)
### 1956: The Dartmouth proposal (origin of the term “artificial intelligence”)
The 1956 Dartmouth workshop proposal explicitly uses the term “artificial intelligence” and proposes a summer study.

- Source: “Dartmouth Proposal” (1956), hosted by MIT CSAIL: <https://people.csail.mit.edu/brooks/idocs/DartmouthProposal.pdf>

### 1986: Backpropagation popularization
The Nature paper “Learning representations by back-propagating errors” is a key early deep learning milestone.

- Source: Hinton, Rumelhart, Williams (1986), PDF: <https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/absps/naturebp.pdf>
- Source (landing page): Nature, article 323533a0: <https://www.nature.com/articles/323533a0>

### 2015: ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) benchmark write-up
The IJCV paper documents the ImageNet challenge and its role as a computer-vision benchmark.

- Source: Russakovsky et al., “ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge” (IJCV): <https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11263-015-0816-y>
- Source (arXiv version): <https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0575>

### 2017: Transformers
Transformers are introduced as an attention-only architecture for sequence transduction.

- Source: Vaswani et al., “Attention Is All You Need”: <https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762>

### 2018–2020: Pretraining paradigms and scaling
- BERT describes masked-language-model pretraining and bidirectional representations.
  - Source: Devlin et al., “BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding”: <https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805>
- GPT-3 documents scaling and few-shot / in-context learning without gradient updates at inference.
  - Source: Brown et al., “Language Models are Few-Shot Learners”: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165>

## 3) Major approaches (what we could source well)
### 3.1 Deep learning (general reference)
A standard deep learning textbook reference is available online (official free-to-read version).

- Source: Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville, *Deep Learning* (online book): <https://www.deeplearningbook.org/>
- Source: MIT Press catalog: <https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262035613/deep-learning/>

### 3.2 Transformer-based language models (LLMs)
The core idea—attention-driven sequence modeling—comes from the Transformer architecture.

- Source: Vaswani et al. (Transformer): <https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762>

Key pretraining strategies illustrated by major models:
- **Masked language modeling** (BERT) for bidirectional representations.
  - Source: BERT: <https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805>
- **Autoregressive next-token prediction** and **few-shot prompting** (GPT‑3).
  - Source: GPT‑3: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165>

## 4) How modern LLM-based systems are built (high-level pipeline, sourced by component papers)
Because an end-to-end 2024–2026 synthesis source could not be retrieved, the pipeline below is supported by **component primary papers**:

### 4.1 Pretraining (foundation model training)
- Transformers are pretrained for sequence tasks using attention-based architectures.
  - Source: <https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762>
- Large-scale autoregressive pretraining supports in-context learning at inference.
  - Source: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165>

### 4.2 Instruction tuning (post-training for following instructions)
Instruction fine-tuning at scale is studied in FLAN.

- Source: Chung et al., “Scaling Instruction-Finetuned Language Models” (FLAN): <https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.11416>

### 4.3 Preference optimization / alignment
#### RLHF (human feedback)
InstructGPT describes reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) using demonstrations and preference rankings.

- Source: Ouyang et al., “Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback” (InstructGPT): <https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155>

#### RLAIF / Constitutional AI (AI feedback)
“Constitutional AI” describes training using a set of principles (“constitution”) and reinforcement learning from AI feedback.

- Source: Bai et al., “Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback”: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08073>

### 4.4 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
RAG combines a parametric generator with retrieved documents (non-parametric memory) for knowledge-intensive tasks.

- Source: Lewis et al., “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks”: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401>

### 4.5 Tool use and agentic patterns
- Toolformer proposes learning when/how to call APIs and incorporate tool outputs into token prediction.
  - Source: Schick et al., “Toolformer”: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.04761>
- ReAct interleaves reasoning traces and actions for interacting with external environments.
  - Source: Yao et al., “ReAct”: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629>

### 4.6 Multimodality (image + text)
- GPT‑4 technical report describes GPT‑4 as a “multimodal” model accepting image and text inputs and producing text outputs (and references transformer pretraining / RLHF post-training).
  - Source: OpenAI, “GPT‑4 Technical Report”: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08774>
- LLaVA describes visual instruction tuning using GPT‑4-generated multimodal instruction-following data.
  - Source: Liu et al., “Visual Instruction Tuning” (LLaVA): <https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08485>

## 5) Evaluation and benchmarks (LLM-focused)
### Classic benchmark (vision)
- ImageNet/ILSVRC benchmark paper.
  - Source: <https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11263-015-0816-y>

### LLM benchmark suite examples
- **MMLU** (57 tasks) targets world knowledge and problem solving.
  - Source: Hendrycks et al., “Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding”: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.03300>
- **BIG-bench** (204 tasks; broad community contribution) characterizes capabilities/limitations.
  - Source: Srivastava et al., “Beyond the Imitation Game: Quantifying and extrapolating the capabilities of language models”: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.04615>
- **HELM** proposes a holistic evaluation approach including robustness/fairness/toxicity dimensions.
  - Source: Liang et al., “Holistic Evaluation of Language Models”: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09110>

### RAG-specific evaluation (2024)
A 2024 survey highlights that evaluating RAG systems is challenging due to their hybrid structure and dynamic sources, and surveys metrics such as relevance/faithfulness.

- Source: “A Survey on RAG Evaluation” (2024): <https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.07437>

## 6) Risk, safety, and governance (what we could source)
### 6.1 US: Executive Order 14110 (2023)
The EO articulates policy goals emphasizing safe and secure AI, standardized evaluations, and concerns including discrimination, disinformation, and labor impacts.

- Source (official HTML): GovInfo, EO 14110: <https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/DCPD-202300949/html/DCPD-202300949.htm>
- Source (public HTML rendering): Federal Register: <https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/11/01/2023-24283/safe-secure-and-trustworthy-development-and-use-of-artificial-intelligence>

### 6.2 US (voluntary): NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)
NIST’s AI RMF Core is organized around four functions—**govern, map, measure, manage**—and frames risk management as continuous across the AI lifecycle.

- Source: NIST AIRC, AI RMF Core (HTML): <https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/5-sec-core/>
- Source: NIST AI RMF landing page (context, release date; notes a Generative AI Profile released July 26, 2024): <https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework>

### 6.3 International: OECD framing
OECD’s definition update page is also a governance-relevant reference because it clarifies what systems are in-scope for policy language, including generative AI.

- Source: <https://oecd.ai/en/wonk/ai-system-definition-update>

## 7) Unresolved / not fully sourced (due to extraction/tool limits)
These are major elements one would normally include in a “tell me everything about AI” answer, but they could not be fully supported with extractable sources in this run:

1. **Machine learning and deep learning definitions** (and the explicit hierarchy AI ⊃ ML ⊃ DL): no extractable authoritative definitions for ML/DL were obtained.
2. **Classic AI subfields beyond modern deep learning / LLMs**: no sourced coverage captured for planning/search, knowledge representation & reasoning, probabilistic graphical models, computer vision (beyond ImageNet), speech, robotics, causal inference, or multi-agent systems.
3. **EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)**: only ELI pointers were found; the full text was not extractable, so the report cannot cite specific articles on prohibited practices, high-risk obligations, or GPAI obligations.
   - Pointer (not extractable as full text in this run): <https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng>
4. **Foundational AI history sources**: key milestones could not be supported with extractable sources here (Turing 1950; Minsky & Papert *Perceptrons*; expert systems/MYCIN; AlphaGo 2016 paper).
5. **A single 2024–2026 synthesis reference** (survey/handbook/standard) for the complete modern foundation-model pipeline: only component primary papers were available.

## Conclusions
- From the sources retrieved, AI is credibly framed (OECD, NIST) as **machine-based systems** that, given human-defined objectives, **infer how to produce outputs** (predictions/content/recommendations/decisions) that influence real or virtual environments.
- The best-sourced technical backbone in this evidence set is **modern deep learning**, especially **Transformer-based foundation models**, plus common post-training and system-integration techniques: **instruction tuning** (FLAN), **RLHF** (InstructGPT), **RLAIF/Constitutional AI**, **RAG**, and **tool/agent** patterns (Toolformer, ReAct), with **multimodal** extensions (GPT‑4 report, LLaVA).
- Modern evaluation in this evidence set centers on benchmark suites like **MMLU**, **BIG-bench**, and broader frameworks like **HELM**, and highlights that **RAG evaluation** requires specialized methods (2024 survey).
- On governance, the retrieved sources support that the US approach combines policy direction (EO 14110) with voluntary risk management guidance (NIST AI RMF’s “govern, map, measure, manage” functions).
- A complete “everything about AI” treatment could not be fully achieved with the available extractable sources: classic AI subfields, parts of foundational history, and EU AI Act provisions remain unresolved in this run.

- OECD — AI system definition update: <https://oecd.ai/en/wonk/ai-system-definition-update>

# Artificial Intelligence (AI): a structured overview (with sourced pointers)

## Scope and limitations
This report is an evidence-backed overview built **only** from the sources that were successfully retrieved/extracted during research. Several important areas could not be fully sourced due to retrieval/extraction limits (notably: classic AI subfields beyond modern ML/LLMs; parts of AI history; the full text of the EU AI Act; and some UNESCO/EU/NIST PDFs). ## 1) What “AI” means (definitions)
### OECD (AI system definition)
OECD provides an updated AI-system definition and explains the update (including how it applies to generative AI systems such as large language models). OECD’s explainer page includes the definition text, describing an AI system as a *machine-based system* that, for human-defined objectives, *infers from inputs how to generate outputs* (including **predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions**) that can influence physical or virtual environments, with varying levels of autonomy/adaptiveness after deployment.

- Source: OECD, “AI system definition update” (definition text + rationale): <https://oecd.ai/en/wonk/ai-system-definition-update>

### NIST (AI definition)
NIST’s CSRC glossary defines **artificial intelligence** as a machine-based system that, for human-defined objectives, makes predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments.

- Source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “Artificial intelligence”: <https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/artificial_intelligence>

### NIST (where trustworthy-AI terminology is being developed)
NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework (AIRC) site also maintains a glossary hub and notes the release of a beta “Language of Trustworthy AI” glossary.

- Source: NIST AIRC Glossary hub: <https://airc.nist.gov/glossary/>

## 2) A minimal history (milestones that could be sourced)
### 1956: The Dartmouth proposal (origin of the term “artificial intelligence”)
The 1956 Dartmouth workshop proposal explicitly uses the term “artificial intelligence” and proposes a summer study.

- Source: “Dartmouth Proposal” (1956), hosted by MIT CSAIL: <https://people.csail.mit.edu/brooks/idocs/DartmouthProposal.pdf>

### 1986: Backpropagation popularization
The Nature paper “Learning representations by back-propagating errors” is a key early deep learning milestone.

- Source: Hinton, Rumelhart, Williams (1986), PDF: <https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/absps/naturebp.pdf>
- Source (landing page): Nature, article 323533a0: <https://www.nature.com/articles/323533a0>

### 2015: ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) benchmark write-up
The IJCV paper documents the ImageNet challenge and its role as a computer-vision benchmark.

- Source: Russakovsky et al., “ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge” (IJCV): <https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11263-015-0816-y>
- Source (arXiv version): <https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0575>

### 2017: Transformers
Transformers are introduced as an attention-only architecture for sequence transduction.

- Source: Vaswani et al., “Attention Is All You Need”: <https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762>

### 2018–2020: Pretraining paradigms and scaling
- BERT describes masked-language-model pretraining and bidirectional representations.
  - Source: Devlin et al., “BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding”: <https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805>
- GPT-3 documents scaling and few-shot / in-context learning without gradient updates at inference.
  - Source: Brown et al., “Language Models are Few-Shot Learners”: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165>

### 3.1 Deep learning (general reference)
A standard deep learning textbook reference is available online (official free-to-read version).

- **Masked language modeling** (BERT) for bidirectional representations.

### Classic benchmark (vision)
- ImageNet/ILSVRC benchmark paper.
  - Source: <https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11263-015-0816-y>

### LLM benchmark suite examples
- **MMLU** (57 tasks) targets world knowledge and problem solving.

  - Source: Liang et al., “Holistic Evaluation of Language Models”: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09110>

A 2024 survey highlights that evaluating RAG systems is challenging due to their hybrid structure and dynamic sources, and surveys metrics such as relevance/faithfulness.

- Source: “A Survey on RAG Evaluation” (2024): <https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.07437>

## 6) Risk, safety, and governance (what we could source)
### 6.1 US: Executive Order 14110 (2023)
The EO articulates policy goals emphasizing safe and secure AI, standardized evaluations, and concerns including discrimination, disinformation, and labor impacts.

- Source (official HTML): GovInfo, EO 14110: <https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/DCPD-202300949/html/DCPD-202300949.htm>
- Source (public HTML rendering): Federal Register: <https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/11/01/2023-24283/safe-secure-and-trustworthy-development-and-use-of-artificial-intelligence>

### 6.2 US (voluntary): NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)
NIST’s AI RMF Core is organized around four functions—**govern, map, measure, manage**—and frames risk management as continuous across the AI lifecycle.

- Source: NIST AIRC, AI RMF Core (HTML): <https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/5-sec-core/>
- Source: NIST AI RMF landing page (context, release date; notes a Generative AI Profile released July 26, 2024): <https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework>

### 6.3 International: OECD framing
OECD’s definition update page is also a governance-relevant reference because it clarifies what systems are in-scope for policy language, including generative AI.

- Source: <https://oecd.ai/en/wonk/ai-system-definition-update>

## 7) Unresolved / not fully sourced (due to extraction/tool limits)
These are major elements one would normally include in a “tell me everything about AI” answer, but they could not be fully supported with extractable sources in this run:

1. **Machine learning and deep learning definitions** (and the explicit hierarchy AI ⊃ ML ⊃ DL): no extractable authoritative definitions for ML/DL were obtained.
2. **Classic AI subfields beyond modern deep learning / LLMs**: no sourced coverage captured for planning/search, knowledge representation & reasoning, probabilistic graphical models, computer vision (beyond ImageNet), speech, robotics, causal inference, or multi-agent systems.
3. **EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)**: only ELI pointers were found; the full text was not extractable, so the report cannot cite specific articles on prohibited practices, high-risk obligations, or GPAI obligations.
   - Pointer (not extractable as full text in this run): <https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng>
4. **Foundational AI history sources**: key milestones could not be supported with extractable sources here (Turing 1950; Minsky & Papert *Perceptrons*; expert systems/MYCIN; AlphaGo 2016 paper).
5. **A single 2024–2026 synthesis reference** (survey/handbook/standard) for the complete modern foundation-model pipeline: only component primary papers were available.

## Conclusions
- From the sources retrieved, AI is credibly framed (OECD, NIST) as **machine-based systems** that, given human-defined objectives, **infer how to produce outputs** (predictions/content/recommendations/decisions) that influence real or virtual environments.
- The best-sourced technical backbone in this evidence set is **modern deep learning**, especially **Transformer-based foundation models**, plus common post-training and system-integration techniques: **instruction tuning** (FLAN), **RLHF** (InstructGPT), **RLAIF/Constitutional AI**, **RAG**, and **tool/agent** patterns (Toolformer, ReAct), with **multimodal** extensions (GPT‑4 report, LLaVA).
